**Variables to Explore:**

**Recidivism:**

* *inc_to_inc_recid_y1*: Incarceration to incarceration recidivism within one year

* *inc_to_inc_recid_y2*: Incarceration to incarceration recidivism within two years

* *inc_to_inc_recid_y3*: Incarceration to incarceration recidivism within three years

* *inc_to_inc_recid_y4*: Incarceration to incarceration recidivism within four years

* *inc_to_inc_recid_y5*: Incarceration to incarceration recidivism within five years

<br>

**Employment:**

*Poverty*

* *inc_above_poverty_y1*: Proportion of individuals above poverty, one year after release from prison

* *inc_above_poverty_y3*: Proportion of individuals above poverty, three years after release from
prison

* *inc_above_poverty_y5*: Proportion of individuals above poverty, five years after release from
prison

*W2*

* *inc_any_w2_y1*: Proportion of individuals with at least one W2 filed, one year after release from
prison

* *inc_any_w2_y3*: Proportion of individuals with at least one W2 filed, three years after release from
prison

* *inc_any_w2_y5*: Proportion of individuals with at least one W2 filed, five years after release from
prison

*Wages*

* *inc_w2_wages_y1*: Income of individuals, one year after release from prison

* *inc_w2_wages_y3*: Income of individuals, three years after release from prison

* *inc_w2_wages_y5*: Income of individuals, five years after release from prison

<br>

**Housing**

* *inc_hud_y1*: Proportion of individuals that received HUD rental housing assistance, one year after release from prison

* *inc_hud_y3*: Proportion of individuals that received HUD rental housing assistance, three years after release from prison

* *inc_hud_y5*: Proportion of individuals that received HUD rental housing assistance, five years after release from prison

<br>

**Healthcare**

*SSI*

* *inc_ssi_y1*: Proportion of individuals who received SSI, one year after release from prison

* *inc_ssi_y3*: Proportion of individuals who received SSI, three years after release from prison

* *inc_ssi_y5*: Proportion of individuals who received SSI, five years after release from prison

*Medicaid*

* *inc_medicaid_y1*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicaid, one year after release from prison

* *inc_medicaid_y3*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicaid, three years after release from
prison

* *inc_medicaid_y5*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicaid, five years after release from
prison

*Medicare*

* *inc_medicare_y1*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicare, one year after release from prison

* *inc_medicare_y3*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicare, three years after release from
prison

* *inc_medicare_y5*: Proportion of individuals enrolled in Medicare, five years after release from
prison

*Mortality*

* *inc_mortality_y1*: Proportion of individuals who have passed away, one year after release from
prison

* *inc_mortality_y3*: Proportion of individuals who have passed away, three years after release
from prison

* *inc_mortality_y5*: Proportion of individuals who have passed away, five years after release from

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
# ### set project path (only need to run once)
# csg_set_project_path(project = "reentry_2030_cjars",
#                      sp_folder = "C:/Users/abyrum/OneDrive/The Council of State Governments/JC Research - Documents/CRD_Reentry 2030/Background/CJARS Documentation",
#                      force = TRUE)

### set overall external hard drive path (which only I can access)
reentry_2030_cjars <- csg_get_project_path("reentry_2030_cjars")

### create list of reentry states to include in analysis
### based on 6 states listed here: https://reentry2030.org/
### NOTE: Missouri and Alabama appear to be missing from file (29 and 01)
reentry_states_to_include <- c("36", "53", "37", "31")
```

```{r }
### import state_data.csv
### file note: confirm that file is aggregated by fips, cohort_year, sex, race, age_group, off_type, and repeat_contact
df_cjars_q3_state_raw <- readr::read_csv(file.path(reentry_2030_cjars,
                                            "2023Q3_state_delim", 
                                            "state_delim",
                                            "state_data.csv")) |> 
  ### add state name using fips code
  mutate(state_name = csgjcr::csg_state_convert(fips,
                                                from = "fips",
                                                to = "name")) |> 
  ### filter on states participating in reentry 2030
  filter(fips%in%reentry_states_to_include) |> 
  ### reorder state_name after fips
  ### and just keep variables of interest
  ### including one sample size var per data series
  dplyr::select(fips, 
                state_name, 
                cohort_year:repeat_contact,
                N_inc_to_inc_recid_y1,
                inc_to_inc_recid_y1,
                inc_to_inc_recid_y2,
                inc_to_inc_recid_y3,
                inc_to_inc_recid_y4,
                inc_to_inc_recid_y5,
                N_inc_above_poverty_y1,
                inc_above_poverty_y1,
                inc_above_poverty_y3,
                inc_above_poverty_y5,
                N_inc_any_w2_y1,
                inc_any_w2_y1,
                inc_any_w2_y3,
                inc_any_w2_y5,
                N_inc_w2_wages_y1,
                inc_w2_wages_y1,
                inc_w2_wages_y3,
                inc_w2_wages_y5,
                N_inc_hud_y1,
                inc_hud_y1,
                inc_hud_y3,
                inc_hud_y5,
                N_inc_ssi_y1,
                inc_ssi_y1,
                inc_ssi_y3,
                inc_ssi_y5, 
                N_inc_medicaid_y1,
                inc_medicaid_y1,
                inc_medicaid_y3, 
                inc_medicaid_y5, 
                inc_medicare_y1, 
                inc_medicare_y3, 
                inc_medicare_y5, 
                N_inc_mortality_y1,
                inc_mortality_y1, 
                inc_mortality_y3, 
                inc_mortality_y5) |> 
  ### now clean following grouping vars: sex, race, age_group, off_type, and repeat_contact
  ### 0 == overall counts for all grouping vars will be NA in clean variable versions
  
  ### age
  ### use factor function to assign labels to values
   mutate(age_group_clean = factor(age_group,
         levels = c(1,2,3),
         labels = c("15-24", 
                    "25-40", 
                    "40+")),  
  ### race/ethnicity
  race_clean = factor(race,
         levels = c(1,2,3,4,5),
         labels = c("White, non-Hispanic",
                    "Black, non-Hispanic",
                    "Asian or Pacific Islander, non-Hispanic",
                    "Hispanic",
                    "American Indian or Alaska Native")),
  ### sex
  sex_clean = factor(sex,
         levels = c(1,2),
         labels = c("Male", 
                    "Female")),
  ### off_type
  off_type_clean = factor(off_type,
         levels = c(1,2,3),
         labels = c("Violent", 
                    "Property", 
                    "Drug")),
  ### repeat_contact
  repeat_contact_clean = factor(repeat_contact,
         levels = c(1,2,3),
         labels = c("First-time contact only", 
                    "Repeat contact only",
                    "All calculated with reweights")))


### create analytic file with only overall counts and rates
df_cjars_q3_state_overall_only <- df_cjars_q3_state_raw |> 
  ### 0 == overall counts for all grouping vars
  filter(age_group==0,
         race==0, 
         sex==0,
         off_type==0,
         repeat_contact==0)

```





# Trends in Violent Crime and Accountability

## 50-state violent crime data

::: {.panel-tabset}

## 2019–2023 change

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.5

# Assign colors
darkorange  <- "#7B3014"
orange      <- "#D25E2D"
lightorange <- "#EDB799"
white       <- "#FFFFFF"
lightblue   <- "#9ed4ef"
regblue     <- "#007392"
darkblue    <- "#00475d"

### add tooltip
srs_state_to_map_2 <- srs_state_to_map |>
  ### add '+" in front of positive numbers and 0
  ### only for value we'll include in tooltip
  mutate(
    viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023_clean = as.numeric(comma(
      viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023, 1
    )),
    viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023_clean = sprintf("%+3d%%", viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023_clean),
    tooltip = paste0(
      "<b>", state_name, "</b><br>",
      "Change in violent crime rate: ",
      viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023_clean,
      "<br>",
      "Violent incidents per 100k (2023): ",
      comma(viol_crime_rate_100k_2023, 1),
      "<br>",
      "Violent incidents per 100k (2019): ",
      comma(viol_crime_rate_100k_2019, 1)
    ),
    url = paste0("https://projects.csgjusticecenter.org/tools-for-states-to-address-crime/50-state-crime-data/?state=", tolower(state_abbr))
  )

# Get data range
data_range <-
  range(srs_state_to_map_2$viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023,
        na.rm = TRUE)
min <- data_range[1]
max <- data_range[2]
# print(min); print(max)

# Adjust extremes so they are balanced at zero
new_min <- min(-abs(min), -abs(max))
new_max <- max(abs(min), abs(max))
# print(new_min); print(new_max)

### highchart
highchart() |>
  hc_add_series_map(
    map = hex_gj,
    df = srs_state_to_map_2,
    joinBy = c("state_abb", "state_abbr"),
    value = "viol_crime_rate_percent_change_2019_2023",
    nullColor = "#E8E8E8",
    dataLabels = list(
      enabled = TRUE,
      format = "{point.state_abb}",
      style = list(
        fontSize = "13px",
        fontFamily = default_fonts,
        fontWeight = 700,
        textOutline = 0
      )
    ),
    accessibility = list(
      point = list(
        valueDescriptionFormat = "state: {point.state_name}, percent change: {point.value:.1f}"
        )
      )
  ) |>
  hc_title(
    text = "Change in violent crime, 2019–2023",
    align = "left",
    style = list(
      fontFamily = header_font,
      color = "#005FAD",
      fontSize = "24px",
      fontWeight = "bold"
    )
  ) |>
  hc_subtitle(
    text = "Percent change in crime reported to police per 100,000 residents",
    align = "left",
    style = list(fontFamily = default_fonts, fontSize = "16px",
                                 color = "#666666")
  ) |> 
  hc_colorAxis(
    min = new_min,
    max = new_max,
    endOnTick = TRUE,
    startOnTick = TRUE,
    stops = color_stops(
      7,
      c(
        darkblue,
        regblue,
        lightblue,
        white,
        lightorange,
        orange,
        darkorange
      )
    ),
    labels = list(
      format = "{value}%",
      style = list(fontSize = "12px",
                  fontFamily = default_fonts)
    )
  ) |>
  hc_legend(
    align = "center",
    horizontalAlign = "bottom",
    layout = "horizontal",
    # title = list(text = "Percent Change"),
    symbolHeight = 25,
    symbolWidth = 250,
    x = 0,
    y = 0
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    style = list(fontFamily = default_fonts),
    formatter = JS("function(){return(this.point.tooltip)}")
  )  |>
   hc_plotOptions(
      series = list(
        animation = FALSE,
        states = list(inactive = list(opacity = 1)),
        cursor = "pointer",
      accessibility = list(
          enabled = TRUE,
          keyboardNavigation = list(enabled = TRUE)),
      point = list(
          events = list(
            click = JS("function(){window.top.location.href = this.options.url}")))
      )
    ) |>  
  hc_caption(
    text = "FBI Crime Data Explorer",
    align = "right",
    style = list(fontFamily = default_fonts)
    ) |>
  hc_setup()


```

```{r}
    ) |>

```

:::

From 2019 to 2023, the national violent crime rate declined despite an increase in 2020. However, there were important variations in violent crime trends by offense. Nationally, rates of reported homicide and aggravated assault increased, while rates of rape and robbery declined.  

Trends in violent crime also varied by state. Between 2019 and 2023, violent crime rates in 32 states decreased, while violent crime rates in 18 states and the District of Columbia increased.

:::

Between 2019 and 2023, the percentage of violent crimes solved by law enforcement decreased in 32 states and the District of Columbia, while increasing in 18 states.

Illinois did not report enough data to the FBI on whether crimes were solved to make reliable estimates.

## Trends in reported violent crime

In `r max(srs_by_cat_us$year)`, `r srs_by_cat_us |> filter(year == max(year)) |> pull(incidents_reported_rate_total) |> comma(scale = 1e5)` violent crime incidents per 100,000 residents were reported to police in the United States.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
  mutate(

  hchart(
```

## Trends in solved violent crime

In `r max(srs_by_cat_us$year)`, `r srs_by_cat_us |> filter(year == max(year)) |> pull(pct_solved) |> percent(suffix = " percent")` of violent crime incidents reported to police in the United States were solved. The percentage of violent crimes that law enforcement solved fell from 2019 to 2022 and increased in 2023 to a level similar to 2020.

```{r }

###################################################################################
### prep df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final for table
###################################################################################

### clean up rates 
df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final <-
  df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023 |> 
  ### recode all solved incident data to NA if state %in% states_to_exclude_from_solved_rate_viz
  mutate(
    across(c(solved_rate_aggravated_assault,
             solved_rate_homicide,
             solved_rate_rape,
             solved_rate_robbery),
                ~ if_else(state_name%in%states_to_exclude_from_solved_rate_viz,
                          NA, .)))

### determine median solve rates by violent offense type for state
### we'll use these state averages to develop an agency-level comparison in the table
state_median_solved_rate_aggravated_assault <- median(df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final$solved_rate_aggravated_assault,
                                                      na.rm=TRUE)

state_median_solved_rate_homicide <- median(df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final$solved_rate_homicide,
                                                      na.rm=TRUE)

state_median_solved_rate_rape <- median(df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final$solved_rate_rape,
                                                      na.rm=TRUE)

state_median_solved_rate_robbery <- median(df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final$solved_rate_robbery,
                                                      na.rm=TRUE)


### final prep df for table
df_nibrs_violent_unsolved_by_state_and_type_to_table_2023_final |> 
  mutate(across(c(solved_rate_aggravated_assault,
                  solved_rate_homicide,
                  solved_rate_rape,
                  solved_rate_robbery
                  ), 
                ~ replace(.x, is.nan(.x), NA))
         ) |> 
  reactable_template(
    sort_col = list("state_name" = "asc"),
    columns = list(
      state_name = colDef(name = "State", minWidth = 250,
                             sticky = "left",
      # Add a right border style to visually distinguish the sticky column
      style = list(borderRight = "1px solid #eee"),
      headerStyle = list(borderRight = "1px solid #eee")),
      n_reported_rate_aggravated_assault = colDef(name = "Aggravated Assault Incidents per 100k",
                               format = colFormat(digits = 0, separators = TRUE), minWidth = 120), 
      solved_rate_aggravated_assault = colDef(
        name = paste0("Aggravated Assault Solve Rate",'<br>','<br>', "(State Average: ",scales::percent(state_median_solved_rate_aggravated_assault,accuracy=1),")"),
        html = TRUE,
        format = colFormat(digits = 0, percent = TRUE), 
        minWidth = 120,
        style = function(value) {
      if (value >= state_median_solved_rate_aggravated_assault & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#15607A"
      } else if (value <= state_median_solved_rate_aggravated_assault & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#E17619"
      } else {
        color <- "black"
      }
      list(color = color, fontWeight = "bold")
    }
        
        ),
      n_reported_rate_homicide = colDef(name = "Homicide Incidents per 100k",
                               format = colFormat(digits = 0, separators = TRUE), 
                               align = "center",
          ),
      solved_rate_homicide = colDef(
        name = paste0("Homicide Solve Rate",'<br>','<br>',"(State Average: ",scales::percent(state_median_solved_rate_homicide,accuracy=1),")"),
        html = TRUE,
        minWidth = 120,
        format = colFormat(digits = 0, percent = TRUE),
        align = "center",
       style = function(value) {
      if (value >= state_median_solved_rate_homicide & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#15607A"
      } else if (value <= state_median_solved_rate_homicide & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#E17619"
      } else {
        color <- "black"
      }
      list(color = color, fontWeight = "bold")
    }),

      n_reported_rate_rape = colDef(name = "Rape Incidents per 100k",
                               format = colFormat(digits = 0, separators = TRUE)),
      solved_rate_rape = colDef(
        name = paste0("Rape Solve Rate",'<br>','<br>',"(State Average: ",scales::percent(state_median_solved_rate_rape,accuracy=1),")"),
        html = TRUE,
        minWidth = 155,
        align = "left",
        format = colFormat(digits = 0, percent = TRUE),
        style = function(value) {
      if (value >= state_median_solved_rate_rape & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#15607A"
      } else if (value <= state_median_solved_rate_rape & !is.na(value)) {
        color <- "#E17619"
      } else {
        color <- "black"
      }
      list(color = color, fontWeight = "bold")
    }),

      solved_rate_robbery = colDef(
```

:::

Data regarding crime and solve rates come from the FBI's [Uniform Crime Reporting Program](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/need-an-fbi-service-or-more-information/ucr). Violent crime includes homicide, aggravated assault, robbery, and rape. Crime rates are calculated by dividing the number of estimated incidents by the total population for a given geography. Solve rates are the number of reported crimes cleared by arrest or by exceptional means divided by the number of reported crimes. For more information, see the data sources and methodology section below. 

<br>

```{r, results='asis'}
cat("## Trends in law enforcement resources")
```

State expenditures include spending on police, sheriffs, and highway patrols. The charts below also include staffing per 10,000 residents and per 1,000 violent crimes. These factors may show the level of policing a community receives, potentially influencing both crime and solve rates and providing insight into how law enforcement resources impact violent crime.  

::: {.panel-tabset}



```{r}
### clean up df for plotting
asslgf_clean_percent_change <- asslgf_clean_national |> 
  filter(year %in% range(year)) |> 
  arrange(year)

max_year_resources <- max(asslgf_clean_percent_change$year)
min_year_resources <- min(asslgf_clean_percent_change$year)

pct_change_spending <- scales::percent((asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==max_year_resources] - asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources]) / asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources],
                                       accuracy = 1)

pct_change_spending_abs_value <- scales::comma(abs((asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==max_year_resources] - asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources]) / asslgf_clean_percent_change$n_inflation_adjusted_latest_year_dollars[asslgf_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources])*100,
                                       accuracy = 1)


change_spending_text_clear <- case_when(
  pct_change_spending >= 0 ~ paste0(" increased"),
  pct_change_spending < 0 ~ paste0(" decreased")
  # TRUE ~ " changed"
  )


```

```{r, results='asis'}
))
```

```{r}
max_year_resources <- max(ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year)
min_year_resources <- min(ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year)

pct_change_staffing <- scales::percent((ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==max_year_resources] - ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources]) / ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources],
                                       accuracy = 1)

pct_change_staffing_abs_value <- scales::comma(abs((ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==max_year_resources] - ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources]) / ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$officer_pop_rate_per_10k[ucr_employee_data_by_state_clean_percent_change$year==min_year_resources])*100,
                                       accuracy = 1)


change_staffing_text_clear <- case_when(
  pct_change_staffing >= 0 ~ paste0(" increased"),
  pct_change_staffing < 0 ~ paste0(" decreased")
  # TRUE ~ " has stayed nearly the same"
  )

```

```{r, results='asis'}
))
```

```{r }
    tooltip = paste0(
      "<b>", "United States", " – ", year, "</b><br>",

    )

y_min <- if_else(y_min < 0, 0, y_min)
y_max <- rng[2] + mult

to_plot |> 
  hchart(
    "spline",
    hcaes(year, officer_pop_rate_per_10k),
    color = jr_pal[1],
    accessibility = list(
      point = list(
        valueDescriptionFormat = "year: {point.x:.0f}, rate: {point.y:.1f}"
```

The following chart includes homicide solve rates by race and ethnicity, gender, age, weapon type, and number of victims. For more information, see the data and methodology sections below.  


In the United States, homicide solve rates are highest when the victim is White and are lowest when the victim is Black. Homicide solve rates are highest when the victim is a woman and lowest when the victim is a man.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Data sources and methodology

Data regarding crime and solve rates come from the FBI's [Uniform Crime Reporting Program](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/need-an-fbi-service-or-more-information/ucr){target="_parent"}. Counts of reported violent crime between 2013 and 2023 are derived from the Summary Reporting System (SRS) and the National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS). The FBI generated national estimates for reported crime and clearances based on agency-level reports, and these estimates were published through 2023 in the FBI's annual report, [_Crime in the U.S._](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019){target="_parent"}, and on the FBI's [Crime Data Explorer](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/home){target="_parent"}. For agency-level clearance data, we used [Jacob Kaplan's version of the Offenses Known and Clearances by Arrest](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/OESSD1) dataset.

The FBI stopped SRS data collection after data year 2020 and required law enforcement agencies to use NIBRS to report crime statistics to the FBI. This change decreased the number of agencies that submitted their crime data and thus reduced the reliability of state estimates in 2021. In 2022 and 2023, the FBI allowed agencies who were unable to submit NIBRS data to submit SRS data again. Ninety-four percent of the U.S. population was covered in the 2023 crime data submissions to the FBI, with most states providing close to complete data. However, the population upon which the estimates were derived decreased by over 10 percent in three states: Florida, Mississippi, and Wyoming, so conclusions about crime changes in those states should be interpreted with additional caution.

Crime rates are calculated by dividing the number of estimated incidents by the total U.S. population. Population data come from the U.S. Census Bureau [American Community Survey 1-year estimates (table B01003)](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/data.html){target="_parent"} and the [2020 Decennial Census Redistricting Data (table P1)](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial-census/about/rdo/summary-files.html){target="_parent"}.

Solve rates are the number of reported crimes cleared by arrest or by exceptional means divided by the number of reported crimes. A reported crime incident is [cleared by exceptional means](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/clearances){target='_parent'} if a law enforcement agency is unable to arrest or formally charge a person with a crime, but the agency has met the following conditions:
    
a) Identified the person who committed the crime
b) Gathered enough evidence to support an arrest, make a charge, and turn over the person to the court for prosecution
c) Identified the suspect’s exact location so that the person could be taken into custody immediately
d) Encountered a circumstance outside the control of law enforcement that prohibits the agency from arresting, charging, and prosecuting the person
    
Examples of exceptional clearances include the death of the person who committed the crime; the victim’s refusal to cooperate with the prosecution after the person who committed the crime has been identified; or the denial of extradition.

Data regarding state law enforcement expenditures were downloaded from the U.S. Census Bureau [Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/gov-finances.html){target="_parent"}.

Officer employment analysis is restricted to sworn law enforcement officers and was downloaded from the FBI's [Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program police employee data files](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/police-employee-data){target="_parent"}.

Data on homicide solve rate trends and case characteristics come from the FBI's [Supplementary Homicide Reporting (SHR) Program](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/expanded-homicide){target="_parent"}.

:::
